messages:
Alex: Heads-up — pushed a small canary for an alternative ROPE/ALiBi kernel that uses adaptive windowing + accumulator clamping. Want quick eyes before we run a larger canary.
Priya: Nice. What's the adaptive windowing heuristic?
Alex: We keep the original ROPE math but cap the phase accumulation per token using a dynamic scale that depends on seq_len and dtype. Rough sketch: `scale = min(1.0, 65504.0 / max_abs_accum)` then `accum *= scale`. It prevents overflow in fp16 paths.
Matt: So we scale down accumulators only when they would overflow in the target dtype? Any perf regression?
Alex: Microbench shows ~1% slower on very long sequences (>= 16k) in fp16 kernels due to the extra branch, but avg latency on our corpora is unchanged. Throughput is stable.
Jia: What about ALiBi? The slope math still uses additive decay; do we clamp there too?
Alex: Yes — ALiBi slopes get normalized with the same scale. Key idea: apply a single conservative normalization per attention invocation instead of per-head ops. Saves some work and keeps semantics close.
Sam: Concern: normalization changes absolute magnitudes, could it produce small distribution shifts that break cached KV similarity checks?
Alex: Good point. We ran our prompt-regression suites (2000 cases). There were 12 tiny diffs — all token-prob shifts < 1e-5. No functional regressions.
Priya: Can you paste the canary config?
Alex: Sure:
```
canary: rope-alibi-adaptive-2026
selector: fp16_longctx
metrics: perplexity, latency_p50, p95, #numerical-nans
rollback_if: #numerical-nans > 0 or p95_latency_increase > 0.1
```
Matt: How do we detect the subtle NaN/Inf root cause? Last time it was an index wrap in the kernel when seq_len % block == 0.
Alex: This new kernel adds sentinel checks at the index computation (cheap bounds check) and an assert-mode compile flag that bails to a safe scalar path if it sees a suspicious stride. Enabled only in staged canary.
Jia: Any interaction with KV prefix caching? If we scale accumulators differently when reading cached KV vs fresh compute, outputs could diverge.
Alex: We normalize based on the global max_abs_accum observed across the entire request (including cached KV). That keeps cache-compatible arithmetic.
Sam: What about quantized paths (INT8 / 4-bit)? Do we preserve the same clamp semantics?
Alex: For quantized we switch to a pre-quantization rescale step. The plan: compute scale in fp32/fp16, apply to float accum, then requantize. Avoids introducing extra bias in quantization zero-points.
Priya: Tests? Need unit tests exercising pathological sequences: long repeated tokens, alternating sign gradients, and dtype path switching mid-request.
Alex: Added three new unit tests under runtime/posenc/test_numerics.py — they run in CI with smoke-rt and a heavy fuzz job nightly.
Matt: Will this change the kernel selector heuristic? I.e., pick fp16-fast for certain seqs and fall back to fp32 for extreme shapes?
Alex: Yes — low-cost addition: if computed `scale < 0.9` we prefer the fp32-shim kernel (scalar path) for that request. That reduces the need for extra branching in the hot kernel.
Sam: Any ops team concerns for Dedicated customers with strict determinism?
Jia: Determinism note: because we do per-request normalization, two identical logical requests in different throughput contexts get same normalization (it's data-dependent), so determinism holds as long as requests are identical. We document this in the release notes.
Priya: Can we add a small regression test that runs 1k repeat requests across both kernels and ensures bit-identical outputs for fp32 paths? Ops wants a deterministic contract for certain enterprise customers.
Alex: On it — I'll add a nightly deterministic test harness and flag for enterprise build to force fp32 only.
deploy-bot: Canary rope-alibi-adaptive-2026 started on canary pool-3 at 1769876601.
Matt: Thanks — I'll monitor telemetry, especially `#numerical-nans` and `delta_ppl`. If anything odd, we roll back. :thumbsup:
